Photograph: Divyakant Solanki/EPA This Is India World news What would it take to make India’s cities better – and safer? After a five-storey building collapsed in Delhi, focus is on how urban areas can adapt to growing populations. Plus, Ahmedabad’s ace newspaper delivery driver goes viral Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here Niha Masih Tue 15 Sep 2026 02.30 EDT Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 07.26 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Recently, I may have saved a woman’s life on the road. Somehow, this was something I had expected to happen. On that day, I saw a truck leave a construction site with a tangled wire trailing behind. I frantically looked to see what the wire was attached to and spotted the scaffolding a few meters ahead. I shrieked and grabbed the hand of the woman walking in front of me just as the metal pipes came crashing down. We hugged for a brief second, and then walked our separate ways. Mumbai (pictured top) is a city that is being made every day, and so much of the Bandra-Khar area that I inhabit is never not under construction. Since I moved here from Seoul earlier this year, I have learned to be hypervigilant every time I walk the streets. I was reminded of that moment last week as news broke about the collapse of a five-storey building in Delhi, which killed seven people. Authorities had flagged safety concerns in the neighbourhood months earlier, the Hindustan Times reported , after 23 people died in a fire at another building . As the world’s most populous country, India can feel like a place where life can be startlingly cheap, and people die every day in tragedies that could have been prevented. According to analysis of government data by the Times of India , between 2020 and 2004 nearly 33,000 deaths occurred due to building collapses, fires or people falling into pits and maintenance holes. The collapse in Delhi has prompted questions, once again, about the state of urban infrastructure in India’s biggest cities. At a time when the country is undertaking a rapid infrastructure boom – new airports, high-speed expressways, luxury residential towers– daily life in cities like Delhi, Mumbai or Bengaluru appears to be deteriorating. Indian cities are not walkable, they rank among the worst for air quality, construction is poorly regulated, seasonal flooding is common and waste management remains under pressure. These challenges are only going to increase; the World Bank expects India’s urban population to double, going up to 951 million, by 2050. More than half of the urban infrastructure the country will need by then has yet to be built, it said. View image in fullscreen The problem with India’s roads begins with on-street parking, believe some experts. Photograph: DB Pictures/Alamy So, what would it take to make our cities better and safer? The experts I spoke to broadly agreed that Indian cities don’t lack rules as much as the political will and institutional machinery to enforce them. For infrastructure veteran Vinayak Chatterjee, one solution lies in giving urban local bodies more power. He points to a constitutional amendment from 1992 that was meant to strengthen municipalities and give them greater responsibility over urban planning. “But it remains largely unimplemented – in spirit and will. It is a serious matter that affects the very fabric of our urban existence,” said Chatterjee, founder of the Infravision Foundation. Rahul Goel, an expert on transportation safety and a professor at the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi, believes the problem with India’s roads begins with on-street parking. “People are using public space for personal use. Everything becomes better when you remove on-street parking,” he said, arguing that freeing up roads would make pedestrians and cyclists safer, reduce traffic jams and make walking easier. In other cities in the global south, from Bangkok to Manila to Cape Town, one cannot just park their car on the road to run errands, Goel said. He described it as a governance failure, saying there is a need to create more parking spaces and perhaps have civil defense personnel or municipal workers enforce fines. “Our streets are self-run,” Goel said. “That’s why they are in complete disarray.” He pointed to the Delhi Metro as an example of a space where people follow rules and things are orderly. “When rules are enforced, people follow them.” View image in fullscreen People vacate buildings marked for demolition in Satya Niketan after the collapse of a five-storey building. Photograph: Vishal Kapoor/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock The same gap between rules and enforcement is evident at construction sites. India has detailed guidelines for construction approvals, including how traffic must be managed, what signage must be put up, and creating paths for pedestrians. But compliance remains a significant problem, says Geetam Tiwari, emeritus professor at Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi. In an audit of construction sites on highways, including bridges, Tiwari and her colleagues found widespread violations. Contractors had a financial incentive to complete projects quickly with payments being tied to the pace of construction, she said, adding that penalties for violations were low enough that it was cheaper to simply pay the fine than make fixes. For unsafe buildings and unauthorised renovations, Tiwari said, the solution also requires bringing stakeholders together: resident associations, landlords, lessees and local authorities to conduct audits, raise awareness and penalise contractors who violate safety requirements. Actions, she said, that should not wait for the next tragedy. In the aftermath of the Delhi case, the high court has directed authorities to inspect student accommodations for safety. Building owners have been arrested and several municipal officials in charge of the area have been suspended. A similar governance deficit shows up when it comes to air pollution, another long-time challenge for Indian cities. Ronak Sutaria, founder and CEO of Respirer Living Sciences, has been working on one aspect of this issue: by developing affordable air-quality monitors for construction sites. Respirer’s air-quality monitors are now installed in 5,000 locations across 10 cities in India, helping authorities identify pollution hotspots. (Some cities, including Mumbai, require construction sites to monitor pollution levels.) “A number of sites are getting alerts [from authorities] and are taking dust-suppression measures, for instance, to bring down [pollution] levels. So, the entire loop is sort of working,” Sutaria said. Indian cities continue to grow, but the question is whether governance can keep pace. On that afternoon in Bandra, I recall thinking how lucky the woman and I were not to be grievously injured. But we shouldn’t have to rely on luck to survive. What else we’re reading about View image in fullscreen Xi Jinping, far right, with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and India’s Narendra Modi at this year’s Brics summit. Photograph: Alexander Kazakov/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool/EPA New Delhi declaration | The Brics summit held in New Delhi over the weekend adopted a declaration with Iran and the United Arab Emirates agreeing to a late-stage compromise on the language about the war in the Middle East. Despite fielding few candidates and evidence of little political activity, the high amounts expose glaring gaps in oversight of political finances. The deadline is 30 September – find out more and apply here . Guest shelf A recommendation from someone with great taste View image in fullscreen Poet Parag Pawan’s book. This week, writer and professor Amitava Kumar (@amitavawriter ), whose latest book, The Social Life of Trains , explores how railways helped shape India’s national identity, suggests the work of a poet he discovered on Instagram: “Can I begin with a confession? I have been a professor of literature for more than three decades, but I don’t often understand poems. How lovely it is, then, to discover a poet whose lines are as clear and beautiful as the dawn! Recently, I came across the poems of a young Hindi poet named Parag Pawan . They spoke to me and, more importantly, they spoke to our moment. I immediately sat down to translate them into English. A series of his poems could be translated as Poems for the Unemployed. One of the poems, sharp and precise, begins with the funny, acerbic lines: ‘On the topic of our unemployment / the prime minister gives speeches / but he doesn’t give us jobs. / He works for eighteen hours / while we believe that asking anyone to work / for more than eight hours / is exploitation.’” Count it A number worth knowing View image in fullscreen Umar Khalid, who has spent six years in an Indian jail without trial. 2,192 That’s the number of days Umar Khalid has spent in jail since his arrest on 13 September 2020 – without trial. Last week, the student activist wrote a searing account describing the daily drudgery of life in prison, published in The Quint . Earlier this year, in his first interview since being jailed , Khalid told the Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Peterson: “Humanity is a privilege that is not granted to people like me.” Vibe check View image in fullscreen World’s fastest paper delivery service? Ayan Shaikh at work in Ahmedabad. Photograph: Instagram As more people read news online, watching Ayan Shaikh ( @paperboy_ayan ) delivering newspapers with serious swag gave me great joy and some hope. The 22-year-old from Ahmedabad posts videos of it on Instagram, and it’s a feat to watch. Watch his papers swerve, reach gravity-defying heights and land with pinpoint accuracy and tell me his deliveries don’t rival Jasprit Bumrah . Delivering papers was Shaikh’s first job after he dropped out of school. He spent four years mastering the techniques that would allow him to make faster deliveries to earn more money. The first video, filmed by his friend, had 20m views and a recent one has crossed 128m, more views than many Bollywood stars might command. He starts his day at 4:30am, making 300 deliveries in two hours, before he begins a second shift as a gig worker for quick commerce apps. “I think people love [the videos] because I do it passionately … from my heart,” he said. “If you do things dedicatedly, anything is possible. It won’t work out once, twice, thrice, but it might on the fourth attempt.” Get in touch Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? https://www.dw.com/en/france-police-clas.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5O0YO Student demonstrators complained about absent teachers, long schedules and dilapidated classrooms unable to cope with rising temperatures Image: Abdul Saboor/REUTERS Advertisement Thousands of students demonstrated near Bastille Square in Paris on Thursday afternoon, as France 's nationwide student protests continue. Crowds of students climbed the famous Bastille Monument. Some waved the French flag and sang the national anthem. Footage from Reuters TV showed riot police charging at protesters with batons as they moved in to clear the square. Across France, some 71,500 people took part in Thursday's protests and police detained more than 500, the Interior Ministry said. France will send 3,000 substitute teachers "within the next hours" to struggling high schools, the education minister said Thursday. "Within the next hours, 3,000 teachers will be joining these institutions," Education Minister Edouard Geffray told the evening news on the TF1 television channel. Geffray said they would be at schools between Friday to Tuesday. Protesters marched toward the Place de la Bastille during a demonstration in Paris Image: Kenzo Tribouillard/AFP Students barricade high school Earlier on Thursday, students barricaded Helene Boucher High School in northeastern Paris with trash bins before police broke up the protest with tear gas. As students gathered at the school, riot police assembled in the side streets. Many protesters wore surgical masks or hoodies, apparently to avoid identification. The school has been a flashpoint for clashes in the French capital and was one of hundreds of schools disrupted by protests on Thursday. Although the rallies have largely been peaceful, some demonstrators have set fires and vandalized bus shelters. Since the beginning of the protests in September, the French police have made more than 6,600 arrests Image: Abdul Saboor/REUTERS In response, the police have used tear gas, batons, and blast balls. Human rights groups and children accuse officers of using excessive force. Following an incident in which a teenager's hand was blown off, the government suspended the use of stun grenades for crowd control on Wednesday. Since late September, when students, most of whom are under 18, began protesting to demand more education funding, police have made more than 6,600 arrests, according to the Interior Ministry. France students demand better schools To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Government promises response On Wednesday evening, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu promised that the government would present "concrete, quick, and fully funded responses" to the protests by the end of October. Nevertheless, student protest leaders said this was not good enough and called for more marches. In a televised address, Lecornu also lamented the "violence, students and staff being attacked, police officers and gendarmes injured, schools set on fire or vandalized, thousands of hours of classes lost, not to mention threats and insults." https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/09/russ.text: In 27 Russian regions, there is a generalised HIV epidemic. This was reported by the Central Research Institute of Epidemiology of Rospotrebnadzor. Scientists use this term for the stage when the human immunodeficiency virus spreads in the general population rather than only among risk groups.In these regions, HIV is diagnosed in more than 1% of pregnant women. The situation is most serious in the Kemerovo, Irkutsk and Sverdlovsk regions.And although, according to the Central Research Institute for the Prevention and Control of AIDS, 45,000 new HIV cases were detected in Russia in 2025, which is 13.4% lower than in 2024, last year a record was set for the number of HIV and hepatitis infections in medical institutions, according to statistics compiled by the specialist portal Medvestnik.Experts record the highest level of HIV and hepatitis infections in medical facilities in 15 yearsThese are the highest figures in the past 15 years. Clusters of viral hepatitis C and mixed HIV plus hepatitis infections predominate, said Yelena Igonina, head of the Department for the Epidemiological Wellbeing of the Population at Rospotrebnadzor. In 2025, eight clusters of infection were recorded in healthcare facilities in Russia, with 104 patients infected.According to Rospotrebnadzor, investigations continued in 2026 into 11 clusters of infection in the territory of ten regions of Russia, where the spread of HIV and hepatitis in medical organisations is suspected. In Moscow, an investigation is underway into a cluster in which 22 cases of viral hepatitis C have been identified. One of the largest confirmed clusters in the past two years was the infection of 82 people in a sanatorium in Kabardino-Balkaria. While receiving medical care, 76 patients contracted viral hepatitis C and six were found to have mixed infections. In oncology hospitals in Kamchatka Territory and Buryatia, 147 and 42 patients, respectively, were infected with hepatitis. Another three hepatitis C clusters were identified in dialysis centres in the Samara and Kursk regions, where 26 people were affected.Experts describe violations of sanitary and epidemiological rules as the main cause of the infections, including the use of single-use catheters or glucometers on several patients. In such situations, the source is usually patients with undiagnosed infections.Yelena Igonina notes that these "systemic and gross violations" have become entrenched in today’s Russia. Although simultaneous testing for hepatitis C antibodies and RNA covers blood, component, organ and tissue donors well, testing for RNA among other categories that should be tested, namely dialysis, haematology and transplant patients, contacts in hepatitis clusters, children under one born to mothers with HIV and patients with immunodeficiency, is significantly lagging behind.In addition, for the first time in six years, two cases of HIV infection via transfusion of blood components were identified in 2026, the Central Research Institute of Epidemiology of Rospotrebnadzor added.When hospitals receive large numbers of people with undiagnosed infections, international HIV consultant Aleksei Verter told Current Time, this means that "the infectious process in the country is latent, hidden" and a great many people do not know they are infected.Despite lower mortality, the number of people living with HIV is risingDespite a decline in HIV incidence and mortality in Russia in recent years, the number of people infected continues to grow, Medvestnik’s authors note. Statistics show that for each death there are one and a half new infections, that is, the number of people "living with HIV continues to grow constantly", explains Natalya Ladnaya.The decline was preceded by a long period of rising incidence, but in the past three years rates of morbidity and mortality among people with HIV have been falling and, according to her preliminary data, this trend will continue in 2026. At the same time, the expert is convinced that there is no reason to rest on one’s laurels, since "the dynamics can change rapidly".In recent years, the number of deaths from HIV in Russia has been between 30,000 and 34,000 per year. This is an extremely high figure, stresses the head of the research department for the prevention and control of AIDS at the Central Research Institute of Rospotrebnadzor. "Among all the countries in the world there are only 15 where more than 15,000 deaths of people with HIV are recorded, including Russia." "The highest HIV incidence rates per 100,000 population in the European region are in Russia, Ukraine and North Macedonia", says Central Research Institute of Epidemiology director and Rospotrebnadzor academician Vasily Akimkin.HIV infection has become the leading cause of death among Russians of working age. Among men aged 40 to 49, more than 3% are affected by the virus, clarifies Natalya Ladnaya, while the average age of those infected in Russia has increased over the past 15 years from 32 to 44. It is also noteworthy that two-thirds of new HIV transmissions occur through heterosexual contact.More than 1.232 million people with a confirmed HIV diagnosis now live in Russia, which is 0.8% of the country’s population, Akimkin adds. Rospotrebnadzor has warned that if current approaches to prevention and treatment remain unchanged, the number of people living with HIV in Russia could reach 1.47 million by 2030, according to the agency’s mathematical model. Under this scenario, the annual number of new cases will be between 31,000 and 51,000, and the number of deaths included in the model could rise to 51,000 a year, which is linked, among other things, to population ageing.In the past seven years, the main causes of death among children with HIV have also changed. An increase in mortality in this group of patients was recorded in 2025 in all federal districts except the Central and Ural districts.According to an analysis by several Russian media outlets, Rospotrebnadzor and the Health Ministry calculate figures differently. Rospotrebnadzor’s data are more complete, as they are based on laboratory notifications of every positive immunoblot. The Health Ministry’s data are based on the number of people who have been registered for regular follow-up care. As a result, the overall gap between the total number of people with a confirmed diagnosis, 1.23 million according to Rospotrebnadzor, and those actually under medical supervision, 846,500 according to the Health Ministry, amounts to 385,555 people.600,000 infected peopleOnly half of people living with HIV in Russia had a suppressed viral load by the end of 2025, said Natalya Ladnaya at the conference "Epidemiological Surveillance of HIV Infection", as quoted by Medvestnik. In practice, this means that at least 600,000 people with HIV "continue to play an active part in transmitting the virus", the expert concludes. Viral load suppression occurred last year in 77.9% of people with HIV who were receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART), and "so far it has not been possible to exceed this level", she says, while WHO standards for keeping the epidemic under control are 95-95-95, that is, 95% of people with HIV know their status, 95% of them receive ART and 95% of those on therapy achieve suppression of HIV replication. As for access to medical care for people living with HIV in Russia, 72% of those infected were under follow-up last year. Despite extensive HIV testing, which has increased by 75% over the past decade and reached 54 million tests last year, effectiveness is declining. In the view of the director of the Central Research Institute of Epidemiology of Rospotrebnadzor, approaches need to be adjusted by increasing the share of people at the highest risk of infection, who are insufficiently covered by testing. Their share has now almost halved, from 5.8% in 2014 to 3% in 2023.But the effectiveness of the work is declining, meaning there are more tests, but testing is increasingly carried out among people with a lower probability of having HIV.Chronic underfunding by the stateThe fact that the burden of HIV infection is not decreasing even as incidence falls is reflected in healthcare spending, stresses Natalya Ladnaya. In 2025, spending related to HIV infection was estimated at 279 billion roubles.In the expert’s view, there is no reason to expect the situation to change; on the contrary, the spread of the virus may intensify among traditionally vulnerable population groups and among people living in regions bordering Ukraine that are characterised by high levels of migration. According to Rospotrebnadzor, incidence and mortality may also rise in the Far Eastern, Southern and North Caucasian federal districts. Bloggers have also spoken about the spread of viruses, including HIV, among those fighting against Ukraine. According to Anastasia Kashevarova, the Russian authorities should "seriously think about it, there is a threat of an epidemic of socially dangerous diseases", since hepatitis, HIV and tuberculosis are currently spreading in the army and to frontline regions, but "will then spread further into the interior of Russia".The Insider previously reported that after Russia’s occupation of parts of Donetsk and Luhansk regions, patients with HIV faced shortages of life-saving medicines. The Russian Health Ministry did not include them in centralised drug procurement, and some patients were given medicines past their expiry date.According to observers, the fact that the healthcare budget is shrinking and all funds are going to the war helps explain, among other things, shortages of sterile consumables in state hospitals.Other Russian media emphasise that most donors financing HIV prevention programmes for the general population and vulnerable groups have left Russia. The country itself does not adequately fund these projects, says Evgeny Pisemsky, editor-in-chief of the queer media outlet "Parni+", quoted by Current Time. With 45,000 new HIV cases detected in 2025, the draft Russian budget for 2027 provides for additional funding for medicines for only 30,000 new carriers of the virus.
